nature-econ-184.title: The contract curve: where mutually helpful trading ends
nature-econ-184.text: Two traders keep swapping as long as they value the goods differently at the margin. The contract curve shows where they could end up. It is the set of final splits of two goods that two people could reach by trading to mutual benefit. Every point on it is Pareto efficient. Drawn in an Edgeworth box, it marks where the two indifference curves just touch and the marginal rates of substitution are equal. Any competitive equilibrium lies on it. Where on the curve they land depends on their bargaining skills.

nature-econ-193.title: Inequity aversion: paying to punish unfairness
nature-econ-193.text: People will pay to punish unfairness. Inequity aversion is people's preference for fairness and their dislike of unequal outcomes, even when it costs them. In the bargaining experiment known as {{ref:nature-econ-035}}, people usually reject low offers, preferring nothing to a small share. In 1999 Fehr and Schmidt modeled people as disliking both being behind others and being ahead of them. Such willingness to punish helps keep cooperation stable, since free riders who earn more get punished. Capuchin monkeys refused rewards handed out unequally in favor of another monkey. The model is disputed: Binmore and Shaked attacked its free parameters and assumptions, and later estimates contradict some of them.

nature-econ-162.title: Harsanyi's utilitarian theorem: rational choice points to adding up
nature-econ-162.text: If a society makes choices the way a rational person handles risk, its social welfare function must be the utilitarian sum of individual utilities. That is Harsanyi's utilitarian theorem. By it, any non-utilitarian rule is incoherent: it will accept some bets that every member of society opposes. A weaker condition, that rankings do not depend on the unit, cents or dollars, allows a wider family of welfare functions, the isoelastic family. One setting within it gives the utilitarian sum; another maximizes the product of utilities, as in {{ref:nature-econ-689}}. Requiring the Pigou–Dalton principle, that inequality is not a good thing, limits the parameter to at most 1.

nature-econ-203.title: The Condorcet paradox: when majorities go in circles
nature-econ-203.text: Majority rule can chase its own tail. The Condorcet paradox is the finding that majority voting over three or more options can go round in a circle. A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A. Democracy therefore cannot simply equal majority rule, which becomes self-contradictory with three or more options. With only two options, May's theorem shows simple majority is the best rule. How often does the circle appear? A review of 37 studies covering 265 real elections found 25 cases, a likelihood of 9.4%.

nature-econ-204.title: Comparing well-being across people: a long-running dispute
nature-econ-204.text: Does an extra dollar mean more to a poor person than to a rich one? Following Bentham, utilitarians argue that utilities can be compared and added up into a total for society to maximize. Diminishing marginal utility has been used to justify transfers from rich to poor, since the poor gain more from an extra unit of income. Lionel Robbins answered that such interpersonal comparisons are unscientific and cannot be tested. Harsanyi and Sen reply that at least partial comparisons are possible, so social choice should proceed on that basis. The dispute remains open.

nature-econ-174.title: Distributive norms: rules for sharing rewards and costs
nature-econ-174.text: A group splitting a prize can follow very different rules. Distributive norms are the rules a group can use to share out rewards and costs. Donelson R. Forsyth defines five: equality, equity, power, need and responsibility. Under equality everyone gets the same share, whatever they put in. Under equity, people who contribute more receive more, and members of large groups prefer this rule. Under need, those in greatest need get more resources, regardless of what they contributed.

nature-econ-176.title: Egalitarianism: treating people as equals
nature-econ-176.text: Should everyone get equal shares, even when unequal shares would leave everyone better off? Strict egalitarians say yes, so their rule can produce Pareto-inefficient outcomes. Egalitarianism starts from the equal worth of all people: citizens should be treated with equal respect and concern by the state and by one another. It focuses on unchosen circumstances that hold people back. Its central problem is deciding which kind of equality to pursue. Equality of welfare concerns outcomes; critics favor equality of prospects instead, such as equality of opportunity.

nature-econ-175.title: Justice as fairness: Rawls's two principles
nature-econ-175.text: John Rawls set out his theory of a just society in A Theory of Justice. Justice as fairness roots justice in society's 'basic structure', the fundamental rules that shape its institutions and so its citizens' life chances. Its first principle, the liberty principle, gives everyone equal access to basic rights and liberties. Its second, the difference principle, allows inequalities only if they bring the greatest benefit to the least advantaged, and only if positions stay open to all.

nature-econ-192.title: The Greenwald–Stiglitz theorem: when markets miss easy gains
nature-econ-192.text: In 1986 Bruce Greenwald and Joseph Stiglitz showed that the welfare theorems fail when markets are incomplete or information is imperfect. When one side knows more than the other, a competitive equilibrium is generally not even constrained Pareto efficient. So a government with no better information than private individuals can still find policies that make someone better off and no one worse off. One example involves the problem explored in {{ref:nature-econ-004}}: because of it, an alcohol tax may be a Pareto improvement by reducing car accidents.

nature-econ-189.title: Horizontal and vertical equity: two tests of a fair tax
nature-econ-189.text: A fair tax must pass two tests. Horizontal equity says people in similar situations, such as similar incomes, should carry similar tax burdens; it links to tax neutrality. Vertical equity says the better-off should pay more, which supports progressive taxes whose rates rise with income or wealth. A tax taking the same share from all is proportional. One taking a rising share from the rich is progressive, a main tool for reducing inequality. Both tests are hard to apply. Defining similar situations is subjective, and vertical equity runs into the problem of comparing utility across people.

nature-econ-205.title: The social planner: an imaginary decision-maker
nature-econ-205.text: Economists often build their models around a decision-maker who does not exist. The social planner is an imaginary figure who chooses everyone's allocations to maximize a social welfare function. The planner's problem is one of maximizing under limits, and solving it for every set of weights on people yields all the Pareto efficient allocations. No real planner could solve it, since that would require knowing everyone's preferences and every resource limit. So economists ask whether decentralized markets can reach the same outcomes, and the welfare theorems answer that question. Ramsey first framed his growth model as a social planner maximizing total consumption across generations.

nature-econ-186.title: Dynamic efficiency: can an economy save too much
nature-econ-186.text: An economy can save too much. It is dynamically efficient when it invests less than the return to capital, so that no generation can be made better off without making another worse off. In the Solow growth model, saving above the rate explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-201}} is dynamically inefficient: the economy could be better off today and tomorrow by saving less. In models of overlapping generations, people may save more than is socially optimal. A 1989 study by Abel, Mankiw, Summers and Zeckhauser suggested the United States and other OECD countries are dynamically efficient. In industrial economics, some argue that business concentration or monopolies can promote dynamic efficiency.

nature-econ-199.title: Prioritarianism: extra weight for the worse off
nature-econ-199.text: Prioritarianism is the ethical view that judgements of social welfare should give extra weight to benefits for people who are worse off. Like utilitarianism it adds up consequences, but it weights each gain more heavily the worse off the person receiving it is. Unlike egalitarianism it places no value on equality itself, and unlike maximin it does not look only at the worst-off person. Critics ask how much extra weight the worse off should get, which risks arbitrariness. In climate economics it supports a high {{ref:nature-econ-746}}: if future people will be richer, benefits today count for more.

nature-econ-180.title: Independence of irrelevant alternatives: no spoilers allowed
nature-econ-180.text: A choice between A and B should not depend on how anyone feels about some unrelated option C. That is the principle of independence of irrelevant alternatives. For a voting rule, it means society's ranking of A against B should not flip just because voters change their view of A against C. Put another way, an election should be free of spoiler candidates. It sounds obvious, yet individuals break it themselves. Behavioral economists have found violations through decoys, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-042}}.

nature-econ-201.title: The Scitovsky paradox: a test that contradicts itself
nature-econ-201.text: A test that ranks A above B and also B above A is a broken test. The Scitovsky paradox shows that the Kaldor compensation test can do exactly that. It arises when gainers could compensate losers for a change, yet losers could then compensate gainers for switching back. The Hungarian-born American economist Tibor Scitovsky set out his double criterion in a 1941 paper. Combining the Kaldor and Hicks tests removes this flaw, but the combined criterion may still not be transitive, so its rankings need not line up consistently.

nature-econ-198.title: The original position: choosing rules behind a veil of ignorance
nature-econ-198.text: Choose the rules of your society without knowing who you will be in it. That is the original position, the thought experiment at the center of Rawls's 1971 A Theory of Justice. A 'veil of ignorance' hides each chooser's ethnicity, social status, gender and idea of a good life. Rawls argued people would use the maximin rule, judging options by the outcome for the least advantaged. In a 1987 study, students preferred maximizing the average with a floor for the worst-off; under 5% chose Rawls's principle. Nozick, Sandel and others dispute his use of the veil.

nature-econ-206.title: The tax wedge: the gap between what buyers pay and sellers get
nature-econ-206.text: Tax a good and two prices appear: the one buyers pay and the one sellers receive. The tax wedge is the gap between them, and it equals the per-unit tax. Consumers pay more, suppliers receive less, and the quantity traded falls. On a supply-and-demand diagram, the wedge-shaped area equals the deadweight loss of the tax: one half times the tax times the fall in quantity. A monopoly pricing above marginal cost drives a similar wedge between what consumers pay and what supply costs.

nature-econ-181.title: The Atkinson index: inequality measured by how much you care
nature-econ-181.text: How much does inequality matter? The Atkinson index lets its user decide. Developed by the British economist Anthony Atkinson, it measures inequality of income using a parameter ε, the 'inequality aversion' level. The higher ε is, the more the index responds to the bottom of the income distribution. The index runs from 0 to 1 and is zero only when all incomes are equal, or when ε = 0. It gives the share of current income that could be given up, without lowering social welfare, if incomes were made perfectly equal. Unlike the Gini index, it lets overall inequality be broken down by groups.

nature-econ-195.title: The marginal cost of public funds: what each tax dollar really costs
nature-econ-195.text: Raising money through taxes costs society more than the money itself, because taxes distort behavior. The marginal cost of public funds measures how much society loses for each extra unit of money the government raises. Pigou (1947) is generally credited with first stating the problem. In practice it can be calculated from the tax rate and the elasticities of demand and supply. It is used in the rule for how many goods open to everyone to provide, in setting corrective taxes on externalities, and in {{ref:nature-val-001}}. A common view holds that the costs of any tax-funded project should be scaled up by it.

nature-econ-197.title: Non-convexity: when half of each is worse than all of one
nature-econ-197.text: A zoo that can afford one lion or one eagle wants a whole animal, not half of each. Its preferences are non-convex. Non-convexity is a breach of the convexity assumptions of basic economics, such as consumers preferring extremes over mixtures or firms with increasing returns to scale. When convexity fails, competitive markets lose many of their good properties: supply and demand may not match, or equilibria may be inefficient. Non-convexities arise with goods supplied by the environment, with other externalities, and in the economics of government. The Shapley–Folkman lemma offers some comfort: in markets with many consumers, approximate equilibria still exist.

nature-econ-210.title: The utility–possibility frontier: the limits of everyone's welfare
nature-econ-210.text: The utility–possibility frontier is a curve showing the most utility one person can have for each level of utility the others have. It is the welfare counterpart of the production possibility frontier, derived by redrawing the contract curve in utilities instead of goods. Every point on it is Pareto efficient; points inside are not, and points beyond cannot be reached. Its slope shows how much one person's utility must fall for another's to rise. A social welfare function picks the best point, where the frontier touches society's highest indifference curve, the 'point of bliss'.

nature-pol-128.title: Tax incidence: who really pays a tax
nature-pol-128.text: Whoever hands a tax to the government is often not the one who bears it. Tax incidence is who actually bears the cost. The legal payer does not decide who really bears it. Economic incidence depends on the elasticities of supply and demand: the side less able to adjust bears more. Smokers bear most of a tobacco tax, because their demand barely responds to price. Owners of beachfront hotels bear most of a hotel tax, because supply cannot change. Over time the split can shift, and economists disagree greatly about how far particular taxes are passed on.

nature-econ-286.title: Nuisance: when your neighbor's activity becomes your problem
nature-econ-286.text: Smells, sounds or smoke that cross a property line can land their maker in court. A nuisance is a common-law wrong in which someone's activity causes offense, annoyance or harm to others, such as a smoking chimney or loud noise. It is one of the oldest causes of action in the common law. Landholders are entitled to quiet enjoyment of their land, so a neighbor's smells, sounds or pollution crossing the boundary can ground a claim. A nuisance is public when it interferes with rights everyone shares, such as public health and safety, and private when it affects specific people. Noise, water and light pollution are among the harms the law treats this way. As nuisance suits became costly to settle, most places adopted rules saying which activities are allowed where, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-177}}. Modern laws protecting the environment adapt the nuisance idea to harms that reach people far from the source.

nature-econ-290.title: The Problem of Social Cost: Coase's article on harm and bargaining
nature-econ-290.text: The most frequently cited work in legal scholarship is an economics article about neighbors. The Problem of Social Cost is Coase's 1960 law review article on externalities, such as pollution harming people next door. Its central claim was bold. If making deals cost nothing, people would bargain their way to the most efficient use of resources, whatever legal rights they started with. Real bargaining and information are costly, though. Many useful deals never happen because of these costs, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-641}}: sorting genuine claims from many neighbors, say, or facing holdouts who demand too much. So legal rules matter insofar as they give rights to whoever values them most. The article showed that a tax on the harm, the remedy explored in {{ref:nature-pol-088}}, is not the only path. Its lesson was that governments should have to show their interventions do more good than harm. George Stigler later gave its argument a name, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-629}}. It founded the field of law and economics and was cited in Coase's 1991 Nobel Prize.

nature-econ-289.title: Strict liability: paying for harm without being at fault
nature-econ-289.text: Keep something dangerous and you pay for any damage it does, no matter how carefully you guarded it. That is strict liability: a legal rule making a person responsible for harm caused by their activity even when they were not at fault. An early example is Rylands v Fletcher. Whoever keeps something on their land that is likely to do mischief if it escapes is answerable for the damage. US courts have treated large stores of flammable liquid in a city, noxious factory fumes in settled areas, and oil wells in populated places as ultrahazardous. Because defendants pay regardless of fault, the rule pushes them to take every possible precaution. It can push hard. Strict liability in US aviation helped cut small-aircraft production from 18,000 units a year in 1978 to a few hundred by 1993. Once a project's environmental effects have been assessed, the principle explored in {{ref:nature-pol-095}} may be used to require strict liability or insurance.

nature-econ-292.title: The cheapest cost avoider: who can prevent harm most cheaply
nature-econ-292.text: When one factory's smoke harms many farms, who should fix it? The farmers struggle to organize, and some may free ride rather than pay their share. The factory, meanwhile, may know best how to cut the harm. That makes it the cheapest cost avoider, the party able to prevent a harm at the lowest cost. Liability can efficiently be assigned to it when bargaining is hard. Guido Calabresi made the case in The Costs of Accidents (1970), arguing that it can still be efficient to hold wealth-producing companies liable.

nature-econ-288.title: Coming to the nuisance: can newcomers complain
nature-econ-288.text: Can someone who moves next to an existing nuisance still complain about it? That is the question of coming to the nuisance. In English law, unlike US law, coming to the nuisance is no defense, and the 1879 case Sturges v Bridgman still stands. Coase used that case, a noisy sweet-maker next to a quiet doctor, to illustrate his argument. Many US states limit nuisance claims, for example with right-to-farm rules that protect agriculture from newcomers' complaints about smells.

nature-econ-287.title: Damages or injunction: how courts handle a nuisance
nature-econ-287.text: A court facing a nuisance has two tools. It can order the offender to pay damages, or it can issue an injunction to stop the activity. Under the old common law, damages were the only remedy; courts of equity later added the injunction. The law and economics movement asks which remedy is most efficient in each case. In the Atlantic Cement case, a New York court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of obeying an injunction. Compliance would have cost far more than the neighbors' harm. In theory, permanent damages should equal the value today of all future harm to the plaintiff.

nature-econ-294.title: Marginal damage: the harm from one more unit of pollution
nature-econ-294.text: Marginal damage, or marginal external cost, is the extra harm to others from one more unit of a polluting activity, such as making steel. Pigou argued for a tax equal to the marginal damage per unit, to correct the externality. Precision matters little. A tax around 50% higher or lower than marginal damages still captures around three quarters of the welfare gain, so broad coverage matters more. Weitzman showed that if marginal damages rise more steeply than the costs of cutting pollution, quantity controls work better than price controls.

nature-econ-295.title: Internalizing externalities: making polluters face the full cost
nature-econ-295.text: A polluter who pays nothing for the harm it causes is working with the wrong prices. Internalizing an externality means making those who cause an external cost bear it themselves, so their private costs line up with the costs to society. Pigou proposed corrective taxes for exactly this purpose, and such a tax remains one of the main public remedies. Pricing an externality at its marginal damage lets producers and consumers choose the cheapest way to cut emissions. Carbon trading is a prime example of the shift toward internalizing externalities. Not everyone is convinced. Mainstream economists favor the approach, but an older critique from {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} questions whether internalizing externalities can really correct the current system.

nature-econ-297.title: Liability rules: take now, pay later
nature-econ-297.text: Sometimes the law lets one party take another's right and pay for it afterward. Calabresi and Melamed described such liability rules as a form of legalized private expropriation, useful when the costs of making deals block voluntary trade. They argue these rules can increase welfare when those costs are large. The Atlantic Cement nuisance case is an example. A court let a cement plant pay permanent damages instead of being stopped by an injunction.

nature-econ-298.title: Transboundary pollution: when dirty air crosses borders
nature-econ-298.text: Smoke and dirty water do not stop at borders. Transboundary pollution is pollution produced in one country that crosses borders and harms other places. Rain made acidic by sulfur dioxide, explored in {{ref:nature-pol-046}}, became a major issue as it spread across borders. Some countries pass their pollution to other places to clean up, which has prompted laws on holding countries liable for damage. ASEAN ministers called in 1990 for harmonized prevention of transboundary pollution, leading to a 2002 agreement on haze.

openers.externalities-pigou-and-coase: A smoking chimney or a loud noise can harm people who had no say in it, and the law calls such harm a nuisance. Courts deal with a nuisance in two ways, by ordering damages or issuing an injunction, and some legal rules make people pay for harm even when they were not at fault. In 1960 Coase's article The Problem of Social Cost recast all this as the economic problem of externalities. This chapter follows that thread: measuring the extra harm from each unit of pollution, making polluters bear it, and deciding who should be liable when bargaining is hard, even when pollution crosses borders.

reviews.efficiency-and-welfare: This chapter has circled one question: when is an economy doing as well as it can, and for whom? Pareto efficiency marks outcomes where no one can gain without someone losing, and the welfare theorems show competitive markets can reach them, but only without the distortions, missing markets and hidden information that fill real economies. Because almost every real change creates losers, economists lean on the Kaldor–Hicks test and the compensation principle, while critics ask why compensation never paid should count. Efficiency says nothing about fairness, so social welfare functions, utilitarianism, Rawls's justice as fairness and the capability approach each offer a way to weigh who gets what. Arrow's impossibility theorem warns that no ranked way of combining preferences is perfect, and the taxes used to redistribute carry their own excess burden.
reviews.externalities-pigou-and-coase: Nuisance law was the first answer to harm that spills across a property line, through damages, injunctions and, for dangerous activities, strict liability. Coase's article The Problem of Social Cost recast the problem: if deals were free, bargaining would reach the efficient outcome whatever the law said, so legal rules matter because real deals are costly. When bargaining is hard, the law can place liability on the cheapest cost avoider, or let a polluter pay damages under a liability rule, as the Atlantic Cement court did. Pigou's approach measures the marginal damage of each unit and taxes it, internalizing the externality so private costs match social ones. Pollution that crosses borders, such as acid rain and haze, shows how far these questions now reach.
